answer_key_points: TRUNCATE acquires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on each table it operates on, which blocks all other concurrent operations on the table; if concurrent access is required, DELETE should be used instead.

TRUNCATE will not fire any ON DELETE triggers, but it will fire ON TRUNCATE triggers — all BEFORE TRUNCATE triggers fire before any truncation happens and AFTER TRUNCATE triggers fire after the last truncation and any sequence resets.

TRUNCATE is not MVCC-safe: after truncation, the table appears empty to concurrent transactions using a snapshot taken before the truncation occurred; however, it is transaction-safe and the truncation is rolled back if the surrounding transaction does not commit.

In addition to the SQL privilege system, tables can have row security policies that restrict, on a per-user basis, which rows can be returned by normal queries or modified by data modification commands; row security is enabled with ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.

When row security is enabled on a table, all normal access must be allowed by a row security policy, and if no policy exists a default-deny policy is used; operations that apply to the whole table, such as TRUNCATE and REFERENCES, are not subject to row security.

answer_key_points: Only B-tree indexes can produce sorted output; a forward scan of an index on column x produces output satisfying ORDER BY x (ascending, with nulls last by default), and the index can also be scanned backward for descending order. PostgreSQL supports index-only scans, which can answer queries from the index alone without any heap access, returning values directly out of each index entry.
